groups.title: People
groups.explainer: What different kinds of good are worth to you. Results are shown in years of healthy life; these say what a year of extra income, a life saved, a happier year and good done later are worth in those. Value judgments: there is no right answer, and changing them changes the ranking.

groups.title: Animals
groups.explainer: How much animals' suffering counts next to people's. Animal results are counted in days of a chicken's pain; these say what such a day is worth in a person's healthy time.

groups.title: Near and far
groups.explainer: Whether good counts the same wherever and whenever it happens.

groups.title: Catastrophic risks
groups.explainer: How likely each catastrophe is to end humanity's future by 2100.

groups.title: Evidence, age and risk
groups.explainer: How much to discount results nobody measured and estimates that are years old, how much side effects count, how much risk of a lower impact to accept, and how soon a won reform would have come anyway.

groups.title: How credit is shared
groups.explainer: Good is rarely one party's doing. One setting splits credit among funders who would each have paid anyway. The other says how much a charity gets for money, work or budgets that others commit only because of it.

rows.label: Give each funder credit for its share
rows.technical: Pro-rata attribution among co-funders (parties that would have committed their resources without the organisation) instead of counterfactual credit
rows.explainer: Many programmes are paid for by several funders who would each have paid anyway: donors, governments, other charities, staff who accept lower pay. Off (the default), a charity is credited with what its own money changed. On, each funder is credited in proportion to what it paid, so the shares add up to the whole.

rows.label: A charity gets … % of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.technical: Mobiliser's share of the good done with resources another party commits only because of the organisation: donations it moves, spending it changes, careers, and the budgets and compliance that carry out a win, each net of its cost (docs/normalization.md 2.24)
rows.explainer:
Fundraisers, advisers and campaigners do good through others: donors who give, people who change jobs, governments and companies that act. This is the share of that good credited to the charity; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

At 100% the charity gets all of it, as most evaluators count. Near 0% it gets almost none, so no fundraiser would be worth funding. The default, 30%, is near what finance standards give arrangers (33–50%).

rows.label: Lives in other countries count … % less
rows.technical: Discount per step of distance: your country, the rest of your world region, the rest of the world
rows.explainer:
With your country set, a life in your country counts fully, a life elsewhere in your part of the world counts less by this much, and one in the rest of the world less again. At 50%: your country 1, your region 0.5, the rest of the world 0.25.

The default, 0%, counts every life the same, as every charity evaluator does.

rows.label: Where you live
rows.technical: Home country (ISO 3166 numeric code; 0 = not set)
rows.explainer: Choose your country if you want lives near you to count more. Leave it unset and every life counts the same wherever it is.

rows.label: Leave out estimates over 5 years old
rows.technical: Exclude models older than common.old_estimate_years from the rankings
rows.explainer: On (the default), a charity is ranked only by estimates made in the last 5 years; one with only older estimates leaves the rankings. Off, every estimate counts, discounted for its age below.

rows.label: An estimate counts … % less for each year since it was made
rows.technical: Annual discount on a cost-effectiveness estimate's age
rows.explainer:
Some charities' estimates are years old, and the charity may do less today. This says how much less an estimate counts for each year since it was made.

The default, 5% a year, counts a 10-year-old estimate at 61%. Set 0% to count every estimate in full.

rows.label: One healthy year is worth … years of double income
rows.technical: Units of value per DALY (disability-adjusted life year) averted
rows.explainer: How health compares with income. The default, 2, follows the charity evaluator GiveWell, whose values draw on surveys of how people in Ghana and Kenya trade income against health and survival.

rows.label: Saving a young child's life is worth … years of healthy life
rows.technical: Healthy years (DALYs) a death under five averted counts as; deaths at other ages in proportion to GiveWell's moral weights by age

source.title: GiveWell moral weights
source.note: GiveWell's 116.25 units of value for a death under five (@moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5) at the default 2 units of value per healthy year; range 0.6× to 1.4×.

rows.explainer: How much saving a life counts. The default follows the charity evaluator GiveWell's values, from surveys of donors and of people in Ghana and Kenya; older people's lives count less in the same proportion.

rows.label: Good done next year counts … % less than good done today
rows.technical: Annual discount rate
rows.explainer:
How much less good done a year from now counts than the same good today, compounding each year.

The default, 4%, is what most charity evaluators use. At 0.1%, the lowest, good done centuries from now counts almost as much as good done today.

rows.label: Lives that never start count … %
rows.technical: Weight on the good in lives the work adds or prevents (rows marked never_started: future generations, births averted, animals never bred); the suffering in such lives always counts; the evaluator view counts none unless the evaluator did (docs/normalization.md 2.25)
rows.explainer:
Some work changes how many people or animals ever live: generations a catastrophe would prevent, births averted, animals never bred. This says how much the good years of such lives count. The suffering in them always counts.

The default, 0%, counts only the suffering. At 100% their good years count like anyone's.

rows.label: Count the people and animals a result adds
rows.technical: Switch on the lives a death averted, a stillbirth averted, a year of contraception, an income raised and a future kept add besides the life itself (src/engine/population.ts)
rows.explainer: On (our view): a life saved also changes how many people are born later and how many animals are raised to feed them, and each shared value of a death, a stillbirth, a year of contraception and a year of doubled income is read with that (docs/normalization.md 2.25). Off (the evaluator view), so an evaluator's own results reproduce. Not offered as a control: "Side effects count" scales it, "Lives that never start count" weighs the people.

rows.label: Lives that follow from one life, low-income countries, discounted
rows.technical: Discounted descendants per person: each generation the last times the net reproduction rate; 0 where the sum has no end (a 0% discount rate, which only an evaluator's sheet pins)
rows.explainer: Not a slider. A person's children, grandchildren and so on, each generation the last times the UN's surviving daughters per woman and discounted a generation further (facts: lives.reproduction_*, lives.generation_years); from the third generation on at the 2100 figure, at most 1.

rows.label: Years a life lasts, low-income countries, discounted from birth
rows.technical: Present value of life expectancy at birth as a stream of years
rows.explainer: Not a slider. Life expectancy at birth as a stream of years, discounted at your rate: the years a person who is added eats animals for.

rows.label: Healthy years in a life, low-income countries, discounted from birth
rows.technical: Present value of healthy life expectancy (HALE) at birth
rows.explainer: Not a slider. The good in a person's life that never starts otherwise, counted times "Lives that never start count".

rows.label: Suffering of the animals one person eats in a year, low-income countries, in years of healthy life
rows.technical: Healthy years (DALYs) of animal suffering per person-year of diet: suffering-adjusted days through the species step, net of farmed animals' weighted pain-free days
rows.explainer: Not a slider. ACE's suffering-adjusted days for a year of the world's average diet, scaled to this group's fish, poultry and pig meat (FAO), times the fall in production per unit not eaten, through the species step every animal model takes (2.4), in a person's healthy time. Less the farmed animals' pain-free days, where you count them as good and count lives that never start.

rows.technical: Healthy years (DALYs) of animal suffering per person-year of diet: suffering-adjusted days through the species step, net of farmed animals' weighted pain-free days

ACE's suffering-adjusted days for a year of the world's average diet, scaled to this group's fish, poultry and pig meat (FAO), times the fall in production per unit not eaten, through the species step every animal model takes (2.4), in a person's healthy time. rows.label: Pain-free days in the life of an average animal a meal spares, in a chicken's days
rows.technical: Chicken-equivalent pain-free days per animal spared by a replaced meal: each farmed kind's share of the animals in the world's average diet times its days alive less its days of disabling pain, at the species' welfare range; wild-caught fish live anyway and farmed fish have no sourced lifespan (none counted)
rows.explainer: Not a slider. The good a replaced meal takes away with the animals it spares, before your two settings: of the animals in a year of the world's average diet (ACE), the farmed birds and pigs and their days alive not spent in pain. It counts only where lives that never start count and pain-free time counts as good.

rows.label: A chicken's days of pain in one suffering day of a replaced meal
rows.technical: Chicken-equivalent pain days per suffering-adjusted day (SAD) of a replaced meal: the species step (docs/normalization.md 2.4) over the meal's species shares
rows.explainer: Not a slider. Puts the spared animals' good days into the meal figure's own unit, so the species step every meal model takes turns them back into a chicken's days.

rows.label: Multiplier on GiveWell's values of a life
rows.technical: Life value multiplier on GiveWell's moral weights, worked out from the two sliders: $daly_per_child_death × $uov_per_daly over GiveWell's value of a death under five
rows.explainer: Not a slider. Models value a death as GiveWell's moral weight for its age (@moral_weights) times this, in units of value. It is the healthy years a young child's death counts as, times what a healthy year is worth, over GiveWell's value for that death: so a death counts as the same healthy years whatever a healthy year is worth, older people's lives count less in GiveWell's proportion, and it is 1 at the defaults. An evaluator view pins $daly_per_child_death (and, where the evaluator has its own, $uov_per_daly), never this.

rows.label: Results nobody measured count … % of what the research suggests
rows.technical: Discount on every part of every model whose outcome isn't measured for this charity (its reach or effect rests on the research literature or on judgment), the same everywhere: charityevals' own models in the row missing_data_adj, evaluators' models by their missing_data.thin_share, 1 − share × (1 − this) (docs/normalization.md 2.12)
rows.explainer:
Some charities don't measure what their work achieves. We still estimate it, from research on that kind of work, but such programmes tend to do less than the research shows. This says how much those unmeasured results count.

The default, 50%, counts them at half. 100% trusts them fully.

rows.label: Side effects count … %
rows.technical: Weight on every row marked side_effect (spillovers to other people, effects on other outcomes, displacement, system effects), and on climate damage beyond deaths in the tonnes' conversion: what reads it reads weight × the amount, or 1 + weight × (factor − 1); the evaluator view counts them in full
rows.explainer:
Besides what a programme is for, it often does other good or harm: benefits to people around those it helps, effects on other health outcomes, work it pushes elsewhere. Evaluators estimate some of these; we estimate the rest. This says how much they count.

The default, 100%, counts them in full. 0% counts only the programme's main effect.

rows.label: Accept a … % risk that the real impact is lower than shown
rows.technical: Where in each result's simulated outcomes the figure counted sits: the share of outcomes below it (the reader's own value judgments left out; a single event's chance drawn as happens or doesn't, so a long shot is 0 below its chance). 50% is the best guess where no such event is drawn, less is risk-averse, more risk-seeking (docs/normalization.md 2.18)
rows.explainer: At 50% each charity counts at our best guess, as likely too high as too low, or at 0 if it rests on one event with less than even odds. Less counts a lower figure, one the real impact is more likely to reach: charities with very uncertain results drop, predictable ones barely move. More bets on long shots.

rows.label: Weigh each species by Rethink Priorities' estimates
rows.technical: Rethink Priorities' welfare ranges instead of Ambitious Impact's species weights
rows.explainer: On (our view): each species counts by Rethink Priorities' welfare range relative to a chicken (facts/welfare_ranges.json). Off (the evaluator view): by the species weights inside Ambitious Impact's suffering-adjusted days, so ACE's own results reproduce. Not offered as a control: the chicken slider is the one animal weight readers set.

rows.label: Value of doubling an income for a year
rows.technical: Units of value per unit of ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's weight on income gains, kept fixed: it defines a doubled-income year, the measure the other exchange rates are set in. Moving it would do the same as moving all of them together.

rows.label: Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂
rows.technical: Mortality cost of carbon: deaths per tonne of CO₂e, from heat and fossil-fuel air pollution

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Cross-cause cost-effectiveness: climate change versus global health (Clare & Vargas, 2026)

rows.explainer:
Climate charities count the tonnes of CO₂ (and other greenhouse gases, as CO₂-equivalents) they keep out of the air. To compare them with everything else, we ask how many deaths one more tonne causes, and value each death like any other adult's death on the site.

The default, 1.9 deaths per 10,000 tonnes, is Rethink Priorities' estimate (facts: climate.deaths_per_tco2e): 0.43 from heat and 1.46 from the fine-particle air pollution that comes with burning fossil fuels. Rethink counts the heat deaths until 2300 without discounting; we discount them at "Next year's good counts less by" over the years until they come ("Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂", 60 by default), as every model discounts future good. Air-pollution deaths come the same year and aren't discounted. The range runs from heat alone (0.43) to the tops of Rethink's intervals (5.1), which is also about what Rethink's estimate of all climate damage, crops and sea level included, comes to in lives.

Each death is valued by the age it happens at, like every other death on the site: GiveWell's moral weights by age (facts: moral_weights) over the ages of today's heat deaths (60 doubled-income years on average) and air-pollution deaths (48: nine in ten are of people over 50; facts: death_ages, GBD 2023), times "A child's life vs doubled-income year", so climate moves with the same weight on lives as health charities. At the defaults a tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air some other way than burning less fuel (a forest, CO₂ captured) cuts only the discounted heat deaths, about 1 hour of healthy life (a charity that cuts one for $1 does about 0.12 years of healthy life per $1,000); a tonne from burning less fossil fuel, with the world-average smoke behind Rethink's figure, is worth about 1.3 days (3.6 years per $1,000 at $1 a tonne). Most tonnes sit in between: coal smoke per tonne is far above gas's, and a US plant with scrubbers far below the world average.

For comparison, the US government's social cost of carbon of $185 a tonne (Rennert et al. 2022) rests on the same heat-death count but values deaths in poor countries and in the future less; Giving What We Can's 2016 estimate is about 50 times lower than our default, mainly because it leaves out air pollution. Climate damage that isn't deaths (lost crops, income, migration) and tail risks are not counted: our judgment, stated as a fact set to 0 (climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) so it shows, and the reason the default is likely low. Tonnes that come without fuel smoke (a forest left standing) count only for their heat deaths; a tonne of methane counts for its own, earlier warming and the ozone it makes (about 4 times a CO₂ tonne at the defaults); each climate model has its own row for how much air pollution its tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne, from the share of its tonnes that come from burning less fuel and the smoke that fuel makes.

rows.label: A won reform would have happened anyway … years later
rows.technical: Years of a corporate commitment's or policy's effect credited to the campaign that won it (years brought forward)
rows.explainer:
When a campaign wins a change, such as a company promising better conditions for its hens or a new law, the change might have come anyway a few years later. This says how many years of the change the campaign gets credit for.

The default is 5 years. Charity evaluators use anything from under a year to over 50.

rows.label: Chance AI ends humanity's future by 2100
rows.technical: Probability of AI-caused extinction (fewer than 5,000 people left) or a similarly permanent loss of the future by 2100, read by every catastrophic-risk model's AI branch; catastrophes the world survives follow by @catastrophe.ai_catastrophe_vs_extinction

source.title: Grace et al., Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (JAIR 84:9, 2025; surveyed October 2023), Table 2, question 1
source.quote: What probability do you put on future AI advances causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species? 1321; 16.2% (23%); 5% (19%)

rows.explainer:
How likely you think it is that AI wipes out humanity, or takes its future for good, this century. It decides how much work to make AI safe is worth.

The default, 5%, is the median answer of 1,321 AI researchers asked exactly this in late 2023 (their mean was 16%). Others: superforecasters in a 2022 tournament said 0.38% and its AI experts 3%; in mid-2026 experts on the Forecasting Research Institute's panel put a global AI catastrophe (not only extinction) by 2100 at 5% and superforecasters at 2.4%; AI safety researchers surveyed in 2021 gave a median of 20% (a self-selected group); 25% is AI safety leaders' February 2026 median for the chance from all causes, not AI alone.

rows.label: Chance pandemics end humanity's future by 2100
rows.technical: Probability that pandemics (engineered or natural) cause extinction (fewer than 5,000 people left) or a similarly permanent loss of the future by 2100, read by every catastrophic-risk model's bio branch; catastrophes the world survives are @catastrophe.bio_catastrophe_by_2100 less this

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3

rows.explainer:
How likely you think it is that pandemics (engineered or natural) wipe out humanity this century. It decides how much work against them is worth.

The default, 1%, is the median of domain experts in a 2022 forecasting tournament (engineered plus natural pathogens); its superforecasters said 0.01%.

rows.label: Chance nuclear war ends humanity's future by 2100
rows.technical: Probability that nuclear war cause extinction (fewer than 5,000 people left) or a similarly permanent loss of the future by 2100, read by every catastrophic-risk model's nuclear branch; catastrophes the world survives are @catastrophe.nuclear_catastrophe_by_2100 less this

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3

rows.explainer:
How likely you think it is that nuclear war wipes out humanity this century. It decides how much work against it is worth.

The default, 0.55%, is the median of domain experts in a 2022 forecasting tournament; its superforecasters said 0.074%.

rows.label: One person's suffering counts as much as … chickens'
rows.technical: Chicken's welfare range relative to a person's
rows.explainer:
How many chickens' suffering adds up to the same suffering in one person. Other animals count against a chicken: a pig, cow, dog or cat as 1.6 chickens, a fish as 0.2, a shrimp as 0.1, an insect as 0.04 (Rethink Priorities).

The default, 10,000, is what people's own spending implies: the extra they pay for higher-welfare eggs and chicken, set against the value of a healthy year of a person ([the evidence](https://consensus.app/search/how-much-do-people-actually-value-a-chickens-suffe/oDz0S0etQuGQE5lGEEOg4w/)). Those studies range from 1,400 to 120,000. Researchers who rate how much a chicken can suffer put it far lower, at 3 (Rethink Priorities). At the far right, animal suffering doesn't count.

source.title: Consensus: what people's spending on chicken welfare implies (willingness-to-pay studies against the value of a healthy human year)

rows.label: A day of disabling pain is as bad as losing … hours of healthy life
rows.technical: DALYs per suffering-adjusted day (SAD)
rows.explainer:
How much healthy life a day of disabling pain costs, in hours. Animal charities' results are days of pain spared, so this turns them into healthy time, and it often decides whether they rank above health charities.

The default, about 10 hours, follows how health surveys weigh the worst human pain: a migraine attack counts as losing 10.6 hours of a healthy day, the most severe back pain 9.2 (Global Burden of Disease; Salomon et al. 2015). People rating a severe migraine during the attack put it at worse than death, about 29 hours.

The slider goes on to 240 hours for the hedonic view: pain counts by how bad it feels, not by what it stops you doing, so a day of disabling pain can outweigh a healthy day. Rethink Priorities puts a year of it at 2 to 10 years of healthy life (48 to 240 hours a day); the animal-focused values use the middle, about 107 hours.

rows.label: An animal's pain-free time counts as … % good
rows.technical: Share of an animal's time free of pain counted as good time, a healthy day at the species' weight; read only by the good of animal lives that never start (docs/normalization.md 2.25)
rows.explainer:
Research measures animals' pain, not how good the rest of their time is. This says how much of an animal's pain-free time counts as good, like a healthy day. It matters only for animals that would never live.

The default, 0%, treats pain-free time as neither good nor bad.

rows.label: One point more life satisfaction for a year is worth … days of healthy life
rows.technical: Healthy years (DALYs averted) per WELLBY (wellbeing-adjusted life year)

source.title: Calibrated on depression: GBD 2019 disability weights on the PHQ-9 (facts: depression.dalys_per_phq9_point_year, depression.phq9_sd) and HLI's 2 WELLBYs per standard-deviation-year (facts: wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year)
source.note: Default = PHQ-9 SD 4.2117 × 0.031 healthy years per point-year ÷ 2 WELLBYs per SD-year = 0.0652815 healthy years per WELLBY (src/engine/wellby-calibration.test.ts keeps it in step with the facts). Stated in healthy years, so the calibration holds whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.explainer:
Some charities report how much happier people are, in points of life satisfaction on a 0–10 scale. This says how many years of healthy life one point more for a year is worth.

The default, 24 days, is set so that treating depression counts the same whether it's measured as better health or as more life satisfaction. Raise it if feeling better matters more to you than that.

rows.label: Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂
rows.technical: Discount-weighted delay between emitting a tonne of CO₂e and the extra heat deaths it causes

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Rethink Priorities, quoting Bressler (2021), The mortality cost of carbon, Nature Communications
source.quote: These [deaths] are concentrated at the end of the century when global average temperatures are highest and marginal changes to temperatures are most damaging.

rows.explainer:
A tonne of CO₂ emitted now warms the planet for centuries, but the deaths that warming causes come late: both Bressler (2021) and Rennert et al. (2022), whose model Rethink Priorities re-ran, find them concentrated at the end of the century, when it is hottest and each extra bit of warming does most harm. Rethink counts them to 2300 without discounting. We discount them like any other future good, as if they all came this many years after the tonne: 60 by default (about 2085 for a tonne cut today), 30 to 100 in the range. Our judgment; no source gives the year-by-year profile. At 4% a year, a death 60 years away counts about a tenth of one today.

Air-pollution deaths are not delayed: fuel that isn't burned saves them the same year, so they aren't discounted.

rows.label: Share of a tonne's deaths that come from heat
rows.technical: Heat deaths ÷ (heat + air-pollution deaths) per tonne of CO₂e, Rethink Priorities' medians

source.title: Clare & Vargas (2026), Rethink Priorities (facts: climate.deaths_per_tco2e_heat and climate.deaths_per_tco2e_air_pollution)

rows.explainer: Of Rethink Priorities' 1.9 deaths per 10,000 tonnes, 0.43 come from heat and 1.46 from the fine particles that come with burning fossil fuels: heat is 23%. Fixed, not a slider: it splits whatever you set for "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂" into deaths that come decades later (heat, discounted) and deaths that come at once (air pollution). Every tonne cuts the heat part; only tonnes that come from burning less fossil fuel near people cut the air-pollution part, and each climate model says how much of it its tonnes carry (its row "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne").

presets.label: Animal-focused
presets.about: A chicken's suffering counts at Rethink Priorities' estimate, a third of a person's, and a day of disabling pain as 107 hours of healthy life. A won reform counts 15 years, Rethink Priorities' estimate of how far campaigns bring it forward.

presets.label: Long-run
presets.about: The future counts almost as much as today: 0.1% less a year, lives that never start in full, and Toby Ord's catastrophe chances (AI 10%, pandemics 3%, nuclear war 0.1%). Long shots and results nobody measured count in full.

presets.label: Evidence-first
presets.about: Only what is measured counts in full: results nobody measured count 13%, and each charity counts at a figure it beats 7 times in 10. Catastrophe chances are superforecasters': AI 0.38%, pandemics 0.01%, nuclear war 0.07%.

presets.label: Wellbeing-focused
presets.about: Feeling better counts as much as the evidence allows: a point more life satisfaction for a year is worth 100 days of healthy life, not 24.

presets.label: Hits-based
presets.about: Long shots count: each charity counts at a result it beats only 1 time in 10, and results nobody measured count in full. A healthy year is worth 2.9 years of double income and a young child's life 51 healthy years, as Coefficient Giving values them.

presets.label: AI-concerned
presets.about: AI has a 20% chance of taking humanity's future, the median of AI safety researchers. The future counts almost in full, lives that never start too, and long shots and results nobody measured count in full.

uov.label: GiveWell units of value
uov.explainer: One unit = doubling one person's consumption for one year.

sad.label: suffering-adjusted days averted
sad.explainer: Ambitious Impact's unit: days of an animal's pain, weighted by intensity and by Ambitious Impact's weight for the species, so one equals a day of a person's disabling pain. ACE reports in it; every animal model converts it into chicken-equivalent pain days before ranking. A model reporting SADs directly is converted as chickens' SADs, divided by Ambitious Impact's 2024 weight for a hen (0.463966, facts: aim_sads.chicken_2024).

ced.label: chicken-equivalent pain days averted
ced.explainer: Days of disabling pain spared, counted in chickens: each species' days times how much it can suffer relative to a chicken (Rethink Priorities). Converted to healthy years with how a chicken's suffering compares with a person's and the healthy hours a day of disabling pain costs.

wellby.label: wellbeing-adjusted life years
wellby.explainer: One point of life satisfaction (0–10) for one person for one year. Used by the Happier Lives Institute.

tco2e.label: tonnes of CO₂-equivalent averted
tco2e.to_common: ($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + $side_effect_weight * @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier
tco2e.explainer: Greenhouse gas kept out of the air, in tonnes of CO₂ or the same warming from other gases. Converted through the deaths one more tonne causes ("Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"): every tonne avoids its heat deaths, discounted over the years until they come; a tonne that comes from burning less fossil fuel near people also avoids air-pollution deaths, at once. How much of that air pollution a model's tonnes carry is the model's own row "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" (air_pollution_weight): 0 for a forest, a methane leak or CO₂ captured at a running plant; the share of tonnes from burning less fuel times how much smoke that fuel makes per tonne for the rest. Methane is valued by its own timing, through each model's row "Share of these tonnes that are methane" (methane_share): its warming comes within decades rather than late in the century, and lasts less long (facts: climate.methane_heat_death_delay, climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2), and it makes ground-level ozone, which kills (facts: climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane), discounted over the 12 years an extra tonne stays in the air (facts: climate.methane_lifetime_years). A model whose evaluator counts air-pollution deaths directly adds them per tonne in its row extra_deaths_per_tco2e (0 everywhere else). Each death is valued by the age it happens at, like every death on the site: GiveWell's moral weights by age (facts: moral_weights) over the ages of today's heat deaths and air-pollution deaths (facts: death_ages, GBD 2023), 59.7 and 47.6 units of value at the defaults, times the value-of-life slider. Damage that isn't death (labour, crops, energy, coasts) adds 0.6 times the heat deaths' value, EPA's 2023 split of the social cost of carbon (facts: climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths), counted as a side effect (the side-effects weight).

daly.label: DALYs averted
daly.explainer: Disability-adjusted life years averted. Converted into units of value with the shared DALY exchange rate.
